subject: Copywriting
title: A/B Testing Headlines at Scale
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: A/B Testing Headlines at Scale.

hook.text: The Huffington Post tested 25 headlines per article. The winner got published. Gut instinct was replaced by data.

buildup.text: A/B testing showed that tiny changes matter. 'How to' vs 'Why you should'—one word shifts clicks by 20-40%.

discovery.text: Upworthy's writers wrote 25 options per post. By headline #20, they found angles they'd never have guessed.

twist.text: Testing optimized for clicks, not quality. The 'best' headline was often the most manipulative, not the truest.

climax.text: Modern publishers balance testing with editorial judgment. Data picks winners; humans set the ethical bounds.

punchline.text: 25 headlines per article. Let data pick the winner.

quiz.question: How many headline options did Upworthy writers create per post?

details.summary: Digital publishing enabled headline A/B testing at massive scale. Outlets like BuzzFeed, Upworthy, and the Huffington Post routinely tested 25+ headline variants per article, optimizing for clicks in real time. This data-driven approach revealed that headline writing is as much science as art.
details.whyItMatters: A/B testing transformed headline writing from creative intuition into an empirical discipline. Understanding what testing reveals about human attention helps writers make better decisions even without running tests.
takeaways: Major publishers test 25+ headline variants per article
Small headline changes can produce 500%+ differences in clicks
Testing revealed that emotional and curious headlines outperform neutral ones

faq.question: How do publishers A/B test headlines?
faq.answer: They show different headline variants to different segments of visitors and measure which version generates the most clicks, reading time, or shares. Tools automatically select the winner and serve it to remaining traffic. The process runs continuously and at scale.

faq.question: What has headline testing revealed about reader behavior?
faq.answer: Testing consistently shows that emotional headlines outperform neutral ones, specific numbers boost clicks, curiosity gaps drive opens, and negative framing ('mistakes to avoid') often beats positive framing ('tips to succeed'). These patterns are remarkably consistent across audiences.
